stem: In an experiment, volunteers are given insulin to produce hypoglycemia. Plasma epinephrine rises about tenfold, while plasma norepinephrine rises only modestly. Epinephrine synthesis requires phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT), an enzyme induced by cortisol.
oneliner: Insulin-induced hypoglycemia → epinephrine ×10, norepinephrine only modestly up, PNMT needed, cortisol induces PNMT → main source?
ask: Which site supplies most of the circulating epinephrine?

whyNot.A: Supply most **plasma norepinephrine**, but lack PNMT and release little epinephrine
whyNot.B: Makes **cortisol**; cortisol only **induces PNMT** in neighboring cells and is not the source
whyNot.C: A **brainstem** nucleus making norepinephrine for central pathways, not plasma

why: Cortisol from the cortex drains through the medulla and **induces PNMT**, which methylates norepinephrine to **epinephrine**. Chromaffin cells hold this enzyme, so they release nearly all circulating epinephrine, whereas plasma norepinephrine comes mainly from **sympathetic nerve endings**.

idea.rule: Epinephrine needs PNMT, found in adrenal medullary chromaffin cells where cortisol induces it.
also: Pheochromocytoma arises from chromaffin cells
Cortisol-poor states reduce epinephrine output
Sympathetic nerve endings make norepinephrine only
Medullary cells are modified postganglionic neurons

stem: A 48-year-old woman has taken carbamazepine for epilepsy for many years and now has bone pain. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D is low and parathyroid hormone is high. The drug speeds breakdown of vitamin D in the organ that forms this circulating storage form.
oneliner: 48F + years on carbamazepine + bone pain + low 25-OH vitamin D, high PTH → which cells make the storage form?
ask: Which cells add the 25-hydroxyl group to vitamin D?

whyNot.A: Does the **second** step, 1-alpha-hydroxylation, making active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, not the **25-hydroxy storage form**
whyNot.B: Make cholecalciferol from **7-dehydrocholesterol**, but do not hydroxylate it at carbon 25
whyNot.C: **Absorb** vitamin D with dietary fat but do not activate it
whyNot.E: **Sense calcium** and release PTH; they do not hydroxylate vitamin D

why: The liver adds a hydroxyl at carbon 25, making **25-hydroxyvitamin D**, the main storage form measured clinically. **Enzyme inducers** such as carbamazepine speed cytochrome P450 breakdown there, so levels fall and **PTH rises**.

idea.rule: The liver 25-hydroxylates vitamin D; the kidney then adds the 1-alpha hydroxyl.
also: Phenytoin and phenobarbital also induce vitamin D breakdown
Kidney 1-alpha-hydroxylase is stimulated by PTH
25-hydroxyvitamin D is the best test of vitamin D stores
Severe liver disease can impair activation

stem: In an experiment, skin biopsies are exposed to ultraviolet-B light in a dish. A vitamin D compound forms from a cholesterol precursor in the epidermis. This compound is not obtained from plant foods.
oneliner: Skin biopsies + UV-B light → vitamin D form made from a cholesterol precursor, not from plants → which compound?
ask: Which compound does the skin make directly?

whyNot.A: Comes from **plants and fungi** in food, not from skin cholesterol
whyNot.B: Needs the **liver** to hydroxylate cholecalciferol first
whyNot.D: The **active** form, which needs the kidney as well
whyNot.E: An inactive **breakdown** product made later by 24-hydroxylase

why: **UV-B** converts **7-dehydrocholesterol** in the skin to previtamin D3, which isomerizes to **cholecalciferol (D3)**. The liver then adds the 25-hydroxyl and the kidney the 1-alpha hydroxyl, while **ergocalciferol (D2)** comes only from plant and fungal food.

idea.rule: Skin makes cholecalciferol (D3) from 7-dehydrocholesterol with UV-B light.
also: Darker skin and little sun lower D3 production
Older skin holds less 7-dehydrocholesterol and makes less D3
Strict sun avoidance lowers 25-hydroxyvitamin D even with a normal diet
Sunscreen reduces UV-B conversion

stem: A 5-year-old boy has tetany. Calcium is low, parathyroid hormone is low for the calcium level, and urine calcium is high. His father has had similar mild symptoms. The cause is a gain-of-function change in the calcium-sensing receptor.
oneliner: 5M + tetany + low Ca, low PTH, high urine Ca + similar father → in which nephron segment does the faulty receptor act?
ask: Calcium excretion is raised mainly because of the receptor's action in which segment?

options.A: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

whyNot.B: Reabsorbs most filtered calcium passively, but is **not** where the sensing receptor controls excretion
whyNot.C: Calcium reabsorption here is controlled by **PTH and thiazides**, not by this receptor
whyNot.D: Handles **sodium and potassium** (aldosterone), with little calcium handling
whyNot.E: Mainly concentrates urine under **ADH**, with no calcium-sensing role

why: An **activating** mutation makes the receptor read calcium as too high. Parathyroid cells cut **PTH**, and the **thick ascending limb** reduces calcium reabsorption, giving **hypocalcemia with high urine calcium** in an **autosomal dominant** family.

idea.rule: The calcium-sensing receptor on the thick ascending limb reduces calcium reabsorption when activated.
also: Inactivating mutation causes familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (low urine calcium)
Receptor activation lowers paracellular calcium and magnesium reabsorption in this segment
Loop diuretics also raise urine calcium by acting in the thick ascending limb
Cinacalcet activates the same receptor on parathyroid cells to lower PTH

stem: A 41-year-old woman has tingling around her mouth and carpopedal spasm two days after a total thyroidectomy. Calcium is low and parathyroid hormone is low. The parathyroid glands lie on the back of the thyroid.
oneliner: 41F + perioral tingling and tetany 2 days after total thyroidectomy + low Ca and PTH → which artery supplies the glands?
ask: Which artery is the main blood supply of the parathyroid glands?

whyNot.A: Supplies the **upper thyroid pole** from the external carotid; it is not the main supply of the glands on the back of the thyroid
whyNot.B: Present in only a **minority** of people and supplies the thyroid isthmus
whyNot.C: Supplies the **tongue**, far from the neck glands
whyNot.D: Supplies the **anterior chest wall**, not the neck

why: Tetany with **low PTH** after thyroid surgery means the glands lost their blood supply. The parathyroids are fed mainly by the **inferior thyroid arteries**, branches of the **thyrocervical trunk**, which are ligated or injured during thyroidectomy.

idea.rule: The inferior thyroid artery (from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian) supplies the parathyroids.
also: The inferior thyroid artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian
Ligating thyroid vessels close to the capsule protects parathyroid blood flow
The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs close to the inferior thyroid artery
Devascularized parathyroids cause tetany with low PTH after neck surgery

stem: A 16-year-old boy with untreated type 1 diabetes has vomiting and deep, rapid breathing. Glucose is very high, urine ketones are strongly positive and the anion gap is raised. Insulin is lacking and glucagon is high.
oneliner: 16M + untreated type 1 diabetes + vomiting + deep breathing + ketonuria + high anion gap → where are ketone bodies made?
ask: In which organ and compartment are ketone bodies made?

whyNot.A: This compartment makes **cholesterol and fatty acids**, not ketone bodies
whyNot.B: Muscle can **use** ketones but lacks the enzyme that makes them
whyNot.C: Adipocytes **release** fatty acids but do not make ketones
whyNot.D: Kidney makes **glucose** in fasting, not ketones

why: With **insulin lacking**, fat breakdown floods the liver with acetyl-CoA, which cannot enter the TCA cycle fast enough. **Hepatocyte mitochondria** convert it through **HMG-CoA** to acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, causing **high anion gap acidosis**.

idea.rule: Ketogenesis happens only in liver mitochondria; other tissues use ketones but cannot make them.
also: The liver cannot use ketones for itself (it lacks thiophorase)
Mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase is the rate-limiting ketogenic enzyme
Starvation and alcoholic ketoacidosis use the same hepatic pathway
Cholesterol synthesis uses HMG-CoA in the cytosol instead

stem: A 38-year-old man notices much less hunger after a sleeve gastrectomy that removed the greater curvature of the stomach but kept the antrum. Before surgery he felt hungry just before meals. The hormone he lost normally rises before meals, falls after eating and acts on the hypothalamus.
oneliner: 38M + less hunger after sleeve gastrectomy (antrum kept) + hormone rises before meals, falls after eating → which cells make it?
ask: Which cells produce the hormone that was lost?

whyNot.A: Make **leptin**, which signals fullness, and are not in the stomach
whyNot.C: Make **cholecystokinin**, which raises satiety and rises after meals
whyNot.D: Make **GLP-1 and PYY**, which rise after meals and reduce appetite
whyNot.E: Make **gastrin**, which rises **after meals** and drives acid; the **antrum was kept**

why: **Ghrelin** is released by **fundic enteroendocrine cells** before meals and acts on the hypothalamus through the **GH secretagogue receptor**. Removing the fundus lowers ghrelin, which helps explain reduced hunger after sleeve gastrectomy.

idea.rule: Ghrelin from the stomach drives hunger; leptin and gut hormones after meals reduce it.
also: Ghrelin is high in Prader-Willi syndrome
Leptin comes from adipocytes
Sleep loss raises ghrelin and lowers leptin
Ghrelin also stimulates growth hormone release

stem: In an experiment, a peptide hormone is added to cultured cells. Within minutes the cells respond, and the hormone's receptor is found to add phosphate groups to itself and to docking proteins called IRS proteins once the hormone binds.
oneliner: Peptide hormone + response within minutes + receptor autophosphorylates and phosphorylates IRS proteins → which receptor type?
ask: Which receptor type does this hormone use?

options.C: Cytosolic receptor that moves to the nucleus

whyNot.A: Used by **glucagon and ACTH**; signals through cAMP, not self-phosphorylation
whyNot.B: Used by **TRH and GnRH**; signals through phospholipase C and IP3, not IRS proteins
whyNot.C: Used by **steroid and thyroid hormones**, which act slowly on gene transcription
whyNot.E: Used by **acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction**, not peptide hormones

why: A fast-acting peptide whose receptor **autophosphorylates** and phosphorylates **IRS proteins** is using a **receptor tyrosine kinase**, as insulin does. Steroid hormones such as aldosterone instead cross the membrane and bind **intracellular receptors**.

idea.rule: Insulin and growth factors use receptor tyrosine kinases; steroids use intracellular receptors.
also: IGF-1 also uses a receptor tyrosine kinase
EGF, PDGF and FGF receptors are tyrosine kinases
Insulin signals through PI3K-Akt to move GLUT4 to the membrane
Aldosterone and cortisol bind intracellular receptors and act over hours

stem: A 52-year-old woman has a large multinodular goiter removed, and the surgeon ties off the superior thyroid artery close to the upper pole of the gland. Afterward her voice tires easily and she cannot reach high notes, but she is not hoarse.
oneliner: 52F + goiter surgery with superior thyroid artery ligated at upper pole + voice tires, no high notes + not hoarse → which nerve?
ask: Which nerve was most likely injured?

options.B: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
options.C: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve

whyNot.A: Injury causes **hoarseness** from vocal cord paralysis, and this nerve travels with the **inferior** thyroid artery; she is **not hoarse**
whyNot.C: The internal branch is **sensory** to the larynx above the cords; injury risks aspiration, not a **loss of pitch**
whyNot.D: The hypoglossal nerve moves the **tongue**; injury causes tongue deviation, not **voice fatigue**
whyNot.E: The ansa cervicalis supplies the **strap muscles**; weakness does not change **pitch**

answer: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
why: The **external branch** runs beside the **superior thyroid artery** to the **cricothyroid**, which tenses the vocal cords for **high pitch**. Tying the artery near the upper pole can injure it, causing **voice fatigue and loss of high notes** without hoarseness. The recurrent laryngeal nerve accompanies the **inferior** thyroid artery.

idea.rule: Superior thyroid artery goes with the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (pitch); inferior thyroid artery goes with the recurrent laryngeal nerve (hoarseness).
also: Singers and speakers notice this injury the most
Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes hoarseness; both sides cause stridor
The internal branch carries sensation from above the vocal folds
The cricothyroid is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve
